title: Why Helicopters Spin Without Their Tiny Tail Rotor | How It Works #4

hook_candidates.text: Stop this rotor, and the helicopter spins. Why?
Why does a helicopter need a second, tiny propeller?
Watch this nose. It has to stay on the line.
You've seen the little tail rotor. It isn't for steering forward.
One big rotor, one tiny one. The tiny one holds it straight.

parts.text: To hover, it has to stay on this line.
The engine twists the big rotor one way,
so the body gets twisted the other way.
The little rotor blows air sideways,
pushing the tail back against that twist.
So why doesn't this giant need one?
Its two rotors spin in opposite directions,

sources: Torque reaction: FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-21B) ch.1 p.1-4: the main rotor causes 'the body of the helicopter to turn in the opposite direction of the rotor' (Newton's third law); ch.3 p.3-4: the fuselage rotates 'in the opposite direction of the main rotor blades unless counteracted and controlled.' https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/helicopter_flying_handbook/hfh_ch01.pdf , https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/helicopter_flying_handbook/hfh_ch03.pdf

Hook ('stop this rotor, and the helicopter spins'): follows directly from ch.3 p.3-4 above: with the tail rotor's counter-thrust removed, nothing counteracts the torque, so the fuselage turns opposite to the main rotor. Shown as a labelled demo on a simplified top view.

Tail rotor: FAA HFH ch.1 p.1-3: a vertically mounted rotor providing 'lift horizontally as thrust to counteract torque effect'; ch.1 p.1-6 and ch.3 p.3-4/3-5: the antitorque pedals change tail-rotor blade pitch and thrust, yawing the nose and controlling heading. US Army ACCP AL0966 lesson 3, para 3.6: tail rotor 'produces thrust in a horizontal plane opposite to the torque reaction'. https://www.globalsecurity.org/military/library/policy/army/accp/al0966/le3.htm

Tandem rotors: FAA HFH ch.1 p.1-5: 'Tandem rotor helicopters, however, use counter-rotating rotors, each canceling out the other's torque'; ch.3 p.3-5: rotors 'rotating in opposite directions to counteract the torque rather than a tail rotor.' Example: Boeing CH-47 Chinook (named in description only; the on-screen tandem helicopter is generic original artwork).
Simplified model: the small main-rotor tilt that also offsets tail-rotor drift, and tail-rotor drag, are not shown.
